title: Thinking About What It Means to Be a Doctor Through My Time at JHU
paragraphs: I have a slightly roundabout background: I entered medical school as a transfer student after graduating from a faculty of science. I have always thought, "Is there something that only I, having experienced both fields, can do?" On this study abroad, I was allowed to do a two-month clinical study abroad at Johns Hopkins University in the US and a one-month visit to a basic research laboratory, and my hidden themes were (1) to move myself "proactively" in a fresh and competitive environment (where only I can help myself), and (2) to reexamine myself during the study abroad and find guidance for how I want to work in the future.

For the first two months I did clinical clerkships in neurology and oncology. In neurology I was assigned to the General team, which handles neurodegenerative diseases, and the Stroke team, which handles stroke, and mainly took histories, did physical examinations of my patients and presented to the doctors of the team. I had the chance to think about the differential diagnosis of types of diseases I had never encountered in clerkships in Japan, such as secondary multiple sclerosis, MELAS, neurosarcoidosis and Balint syndrome, and to look up papers on those cases. I was also able to perform highly invasive procedures such as lumbar puncture under a doctor's supervision. In oncology I was assigned to the Leukemia team, which handles hematologic malignancies, and the Solid tumor team, which handles solid tumors, and learned about treatment guidelines for cancer, differences from Japan in the insurance system, and holistic care for terminal cancer patients. What I think I strongly acquired here was "proactivity." At the beginning of the study abroad, doing a clerkship in another language was not easy, even for a single presentation to the team required at the morning rounds. The local students were also at a high level, and I was overwhelmed by their drive to improve and their ability to appeal in order to get good evaluations. Feeling that with a passive attitude I would be treated like a guest forever, I told my supervising doctors "what I can do, and what I cannot do but want to learn," and received feedback each time. Perhaps this attitude was recognised by the team, and I could feel that the range of things I was allowed to do gradually widened (starting with procedures, and including consults to other departments, submitting specimens, short talks and so on).

The period prescribed as a partner school was two months, but I applied on my own to the laboratory of 井上尊生, a Japanese researcher who is active as a professor at Johns Hopkins University, and belonged to it for the rest of my stay. I gave a presentation and had discussions on the basic research I am currently doing at Nagoya University (during the formation of the cortical layer structure, differentiating cells limit the range of the elevator movement of neural stem cells and help normal brain formation), and learned the methods of analysing cell chemotaxis, the laboratory's theme. Although it was not a joint study, after returning to Japan I was able to publish a peer-reviewed paper on the research theme I am working on at Nagoya University, as first author, in the international journal Development. During the stay, by visiting a department that collaborates with a pharmaceutical company and by interviewing doctors working as researchers in the US, I was able to look at ways of working that are not limited to Japanese hospitals, which I think was also good.

And regarding how I want to work in the future, there is one episode that left an impression on me. During my clerkship in oncology, I had the opportunity to be in charge of a woman in her twenties with terminal liver cancer (a special type of cancer not seen in Japan). Her cancer had recurred repeatedly since her teens, and had finally become refractory to chemotherapy and unresectable; when I was in charge, she could hardly walk because of edema, could not breathe adequately, and was managed on a ventilator. Her parents and siblings came to her room every day and encouraged her. Her mother never showed tears in front of her and looked after her needs. The medical team had judged that she had to choose palliative care, and she and her family had to accept it. One day while I was in charge, during the team's rounds of her room, I could not stop myself from crying. Seeing this, her mother followed me out of the room, crying, held my hand and said "Thank you." There was no language barrier. Until the day she went to the hospice, I was in charge of her and her family and continued to interact with them. I believe that medical professionals should give patients every treatment they can, but it is up to the patient to choose how to live, and I felt that we must not forget the attitude of thinking about that choice from the same eye level and seeing out their life. It made me think about the value of a doctor that will not be lost in a society that will continue to change.
